messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] RStudio + INLA using Docker
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] RStudio + INLA using Docker
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I've been using INLA on my Debian Stretch based for a year now, where I compiled INLA from source code, and it works amazingly well (and performs much faster as well since I compiled it from source). Here's the Makefile I've been using more recently: https://gist.github.com/sadatnfs/6b15bdc68b2224b19853121a9e1bfcbb

Note that this is using a fork from the original INLA repo, because of a small fix they haven't yet implemented in the Makefile for inlaprog (linking Pardiso). This build combined with R-3.5.0 built from source, GCC/G++ 8.1.0, and MKL linked BLAS/LAPACK is a beast indeed. Hopefully this helps somewhat!

Nafis

messages.subject: What does "max.logdens= -1.#IND00" mean?
messages.subject_clean: What does "max.logdens= -1.#IND00" mean?
messages.body_plain:
When INLA states "max.logdens= -1.#IND00" at the start of the first iteration, that is a bad indication of getting the model solved.
But what is the source of the problem?

In some cases I have avoided this by making priors more informative. Are there other possible cures?

Best
Øyvind

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] What does "max.logdens= -1.#IND00" mean?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] What does "max.logdens= -1.#IND00" mean?
messages.body_plain:
On Sun, 2018-06-03 at 06:03 -0700, Øyvind wrote:
> When INLA states "max.logdens= -1.#IND00" at the start of the first
> iteration, that is a bad indication of getting the model solved.
> But what is the source of the problem?
>
> In some cases I have avoided this by making priors more informative.
> Are there other possible cures?
>

I havnt seen it like this, but it seems like Inf to me. It simply mean
that the first function evaluation (log marginal posterior (theta)),
returns Inf. this is, almost always, due to some kind of overflow from
the likelihood part, or some bad initial values for the hyperpar. INLA
computes reasonable initial values for the latent field automatically
(but better in the testing version than the stable one).

It is often a consequence of a to loose model with not much information
in the data. Yes, more informative priors will help.

It is possible to restart, using  this sequence for hard problems

r = inla(<very informative priors>)
r = inla(<normal priors>, control.mode = list(result = r,
restart=TRUE))

restarting from the previous model. one can also add
control.inla = list(stratgy='gaussian',int.strategy='eb')

to speedup the first step

H

--
Håvard Rue
Helpdesk
he...@r-inla.org

messages.body_plain:
Another idea would be to just change the initial values of the inla run, either by guesstimating reasonable values for the internal representation of the hyperpar, or by picking randomly from a Gaussian until the model runs.

Since INLA does a gradient descent type, where you start should not matter, as long as you do not start in a numerically ill defined place.

PS: Did you scale your data so it contains only reasonable sized values?

Best,
Haakon

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] What does "max.logdens= -1.#IND00" mean?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] What does "max.logdens= -1.#IND00" mean?
messages.body_plain:
Technically speaking, #IND00 is a NaN value ("indeterminate"), and
infinity would be #INF00, but the root cause would be similar;
  sqrt(negative), log(negative), 0/0 all produce various NaN:s (the
IEEE standard has more than one NaN...)
  1/0 produces +Inf
  (-1)/0 produces -Inf

And I concur with both Haavard and Haakon; an initial run with more
informative priors helps to find a better starting point for the
"real" run.  Also, user-specified priors may have probability mass
away from the default initial optimisation starting point, so when
specifying priors, do check that the (default or use-specified)
initial value makes sense...

Finn

messages.subject: Generate samples from log-volatility of SV models
messages.subject_clean: Generate samples from log-volatility of SV models
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone!

I've been using INLA to fit a simple stochastic volatility model, with Student-t distribution. However, I was trying to generate samples from the log-volatility with the inla.rmarginal method, using the marginal from the log-volatility, which I suppose is the inla.hyperpar$marginals.random. I can also see that the method marginals.random contains several indexes, for example inla.hyperpar$marginals.random[[1]]$index.1 up to 1400 (which is my series length). Unlike the other hyperparameters, I'm not being able to get those samples.

So my question is, am I going to the right direction or should I try something different?

Thanks in advance,
Marcos

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Generate samples from log-volatility of SV models
messages.body_plain:
Hi

the inla.rmarginal will generate samples for on marginal. if you want
samples from the joint fitted model, you have to use
inla.posterior.sample() or inla.hyperpar.sample(). see their help
pages. you may want to compute also the marginals for the linear
predictor, by setting the option control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE)

H

Hi all,

I am new to INLA, but I have spent the last couple of weeks reading and playing with the various tutorials and the documentation. I feel that I have got to grips with the basics of the software. Thanks to you all for producing so much awesome documentation for this amazing package!

I would like to ask you experts and other users for some guidance and advice on my model. I apologise that this is such a long post! Please just respond to whatever you can/have time to.

My model is a species distribution model predicting the probability of occurrence of a species of insect as a function of various bioclimatic and demographic variables at a global scale. The data are presence/absence (~15,000 observations). The covariates are mostly raster data with a 5km*5km global resolution (WorldClim). The model has a binomial likelihood, some fixed effects covariates and a barrier.model spde spatial random effect:

y ~ b0 + BIOC_1 + BIOC_2 + ... + BIOC_p + f(s, model = barrier.spde) - 1

I have quite a few questions(!), but first I would like to ask for some advice on mesh building at a global scale.

To start with I took a shapefile of global coastlines. I simplified the polygons (using gSimplify from rgeos) and removed all the small islands below a specific area size. The aim of this was to try to avoid too complex a shape, so I can achieve nice uniform triangulation in my sampling domain. I then used these spatial polygons to define the inner boundary of the mesh, and used the observation points as initial vertices for the triangles. (Currently I am using decimal degrees, which I appreciate is inappropriate at a global scale, but I just wanted to get my head around the mesh building before implementing the spherical mesh).

## Domain boundary

  bndry <- inla.sp2segment(

  shape,

  crs = crs(shape)

)

## Mesh

mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(

  loc = coords.est,

  boundary = bndry,

  cutoff = max.edge.length/5,

  max.edge = c(1, 5) * max.edge.length,

  min.angle = 21

)

However, the observations have a pretty extreme non-random distribution. They are very clumped in certain areas. Using these locations as initial vertices seemed to be problematic, resulting in very high number of triangles and general bad mesh patterns (even when using a relatively high cutoff).

Next, after reading Finn's recommendation in this post <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/r-inla-discussion-group/continental$20mesh%7Csort:date/r-inla-discussion-group/RqZ5v8jCkzo/sd0KBphhCQAJ>, I decided to try a uniform inner triangulation (not using the observation points). This reduced the number of triangles and I can produce what I think seems like an OK mesh. After first running the model with a relatively coarse mesh to get an idea of the spatial range, the final mesh$n is ~10,000. (with an estimated spatial range of 10 degrees and max.edge = ~2 degrees).

Then I ran my model using int.strategy = "eb", strategy = "gaussian"  and diagonal = 1000 to get some computationally cheap initial values to feed the proper model (using auto and simplified lapace) and every seems good, but then when I run the proper model, it seems to struggle. I get the 'stupid search' and my DIC is inf. This made me wonder that my mesh is too poor and it is causing numerical issues?

So, worried that my mesh is too complex. I read this post <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/r-inla-discussion-group/continental$20mesh%7Csort:date/r-inla-discussion-group/H9FymT0DhSU/1ZJ0tKxdbXoJ>, and tried defining an arbitrary nonconvex hull as my boundary, rather than the shapefile itself.

## Non-convex hull domain boundary

nc.hull <- inla.nonconvex.hull(

            coords.est,

            convex = 3,

            concave = 3,

            resolution = 150)

## Mesh.nc

mesh.nc <http://mesh.nc> <- inla.mesh.2d(

  boundary = nc.hull,

  cutoff = max.edge.length/5,  # make max.edge/5 for full resolution

  max.edge = c(1, 3) * max.edge.length,

  # offset = 1, #c(max.edge.length, outer.boundary),

  min.angle = 20

)

This results in a mesh$n of ~5000 and a much more uniform 'good' look. But I am worried that altering the geographic structure makes the barrier method somewhat pointless?

I would really appreciate some guidance or insight on the best way to approach this mesh building. I would like to be able to find the good trade-off between mesh complexity and computational expense! Apologies if I have made any glaring errors or oversights...

and apologies for rambling...

Thanks for taking the time to read this far :)

Cheers,

Mike

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Mesh building on a global scale
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Mesh building on a global scale
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

the main effect of the barrier model is to eliminate the Neumann
boundary effects at the edge of a mesh by allowing the parameters to
change outside a domain of interest instead of just extending the mesh
beyond the domain of interest (which can't be done when the domain
extension would intrude on the domain of interest, such as for
islands, peninsulas, etc).  The number, sizes, and shapes of triangles
instead controls the numerical approximation properties of the
resulting discretised model, in much the same way for both
alternatives for handling the boundary, so they can largely be treated
as unrelated issues.

As long as the geometry used to define the barrier in the barrier
model is close enough to your real geometry you should be fine.  It is
relatively safe to move a _convex_ boundary outwards for the barrier
model, but it's
concave parts (like islands) where you would get noticeable
differences when over-simplifying the boundary/barrier.

I'd recommend taking a look at the meshbuilder() tool for
interactively exploring mesh quality in relation to computational
approximation properties.
The important parts can also be accessed directly for any mesh,
through the inla.mesh.assessment() function, that evaluates the
pointwise standard deviations
for a specified correlation range in a basic SPDE/GMRF/Matern model.
A numerically accurate model would have a constant variance throughout
the domain of interest.
The barrier models are a bit more forgiving at the barriers, but the
tool should still give a good idea of the required triangle sizes.
The usually appropriate quantity to plot is "sd.dev <http://sd.dev>", which is an
estimate of the ratio between the pointwise variances of the discrete
model and the desired continuous domain model.
Currently, the function returns "sd", "sd.dev <http://sd.dev>", and "edge.len", which
is the average triangle edge length near each location (mostly just
informational).

The example below uses the ggplot2 features from inlabru (see
http://github.com/fbachl/inlabru for installation instructions; either
CRAN or the more bug-fixed development version) to illustrate this.
(The interactive meshbuilder tool has more options, but doesn't handle
spherical meshes; inla.mesh.assessment also doesn't fully handle that
case, but will currently just show you one side of the sphere...)

bnd <- inla.mesh.segment(cbind(c(0, 10, 10, 0, 0),
                               c(0, 0, 10, 10, 0)), bnd = TRUE)
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary = bnd, max.edge = 1)
out <- inla.mesh.assessment(mesh, spatial.range = 3, alpha = 2)

ggplot2::ggplot() + inlabru::gg(out, mapping=aes_(col=~sd.dev <http://sd.dev>))

To build a spherical mesh, you just need to convert the
longitude-latitude cutoff&max.edge parameters to radians (multiply by
pi/180), and supply
  crs = inla.CRS("sphere")
to inla.mesh.2d(), which will automatically transform inputs with
proper crs info (so you'll need to specify a crs=inla.CRS("longlat")
when you construct the nonconvex hull).

One can in principle compute the same assessment directly for the
chosen barrier model, but the barrier models weren't around when the
meshbuilder assessment code was written, so it needs to go on the TODO
list.

Finn

messages.subject: Time series constraints questions
messages.subject_clean: Time series constraints questions
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I had two questions on time series modelling in INLA. The first question relates to how to constrain a specific parameter to be zero in a time series framework. For example take a simple time series model y_t = mu_t + eps_t, and mu_t being a random walk;

# Make data
 library(INLA)
y = c(0.2,0.4,0.3,0.5,0.7,1.3,1.5,1.2,1.9)
t = c(1,1,3,4,6,6,6,7,8)
yX    <-  as.data.frame(cbind(y,t))

# Without Constant
formula = y ~ -1 + f(t, model="rw1", constr=FALSE, values = seq(1,8,1)  )
mod =  inla(formula, family="gaussian", data = yX)
summary(mod)

# With Constant
formula = y ~ f(t, model="rw1", constr=FALSE, values = seq(1,8,1)  )
mod =  inla(formula, family="gaussian", data = yX)
summary(mod)

(Please don't take the results to literal, its just used as a way to show the coding...)
t is the time indicator running from t=1,...,T.
Note that the standard error on the constant in the second model is `through the roof' since there is a perfect collinearity issue.
I do not want zero-sum constrain on my parameters. However, in order to identify the second model (so with the constant) I would like the constraint in such a way that mu_{t=1} equals 0. It should not really matter for the results, but its a bit more custom to do it that way in time series literature. I have difficulty finding a way to do that...

Suppose I find a way to do that, than my second question would be on how multiple trends can share the same variance parameter? For example (now without data) I have;
formula = y ~ f(t1, w1, model="rw1", constr=FALSE)  + f(t2, w2, model="rw1", constr=FALSE)

where t1 = t2 = t (from previous example), and w1 and w2 are selection vectors (only containing 1/0s) depending on which time trend the y variable loads onto. (That is the correct way of doing it, right?)
So again, my question would be, how can I ensure that both f()s share the same variance paramater / precision `tau'?
Many thanks in advance,
Alex

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Time series constraints questions
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Time series constraints questions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Alex,

for the constraint, use the "extraconstr" parameter to set an
arbitrary linear constraint. In your example:

  extraconstr = list(A = t(rep(c(1, 0), c(1, T-1)), e = 0)

should do the trick.

For the second issue, you have a case with two realisations of the
same model, which can be done with the "replicate" feature:

  f(t, model="rw1", replicate=w1*1 + w2*2, constr=FALSE, extraconstr =
[as above])

The replicate parameter is a vector indexing into the different
replications, i.e. selecting between replicate 1 and replicate 2.
The resulting random effect vector will have length T*2, with the
replicates following eachother.

I notice that the documentation for replicate just says "We need to
write documentation here.", but certainly not very useful. ;)

Note: I haven't checked the interaction between extraconstr and
replicate; you might need to extend the specification to cover the
entire T*2 size model
  extraconstr = list(A = t(rep(c(1, 0, 1, 0), c(1, T-1, 1, T-1)), e = 0)

Finn

messages.subject: Cauchy distribution
messages.subject_clean: Cauchy distribution
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to get likelihood family to a distribution that is more similar to a Cauchy distribution. The Gaussian is doing an ok job at representing the data i have but i feel the model would be much stronger with fatter tails. I have tried the T distribution but the tails ended no different than the Gaussian, this may be due to the large data set. Is there any suggestions on how I may work this. I saw how to use the half cauchy for priors but feel that with my kinda model working with the likelihoods would be best.

Thanks for any help.

kick1 <- pledgedUSD ~ goal + Twords + City_Pop + Length_of_kick +
  Days_spent_making_campign  + Categories + County +
  f(state_codes, model = "bym", graph = USA.adj, diagonal = 1e-4) +
  f(year, model = "rw2", diagonal = 1e-4) +
  f(year1, model = "iid") +
  f(state_codes1, model = "besag" , graph = USA.adj, diagonal = 1e-4,
    group = year2,
    control.group = list(model = "rw2"))

mod.climbUSD <- inla(kick1, family = "gaussian", data = t23,
                  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
                  control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, cpo = TRUE),
                  control.inla = list(cmin = 0),
                  verbose = TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
to follow up this discussion,

y = c(0.2,0.4,0.3,0.5,0.7,1.3,1.5,1.2,1.9)
t = c(1,1,3,4,6,6,6,7,8)
yX    <-  as.data.frame(cbind(y,t))

econstr = list(A = matrix(c(1,rep(0,7)), 1, 8), e=0)
# With Constant
formula = y ~ f(t, model="rw1", constr=FALSE, values = seq(1,8,1),
extraconstr = econstr)

mod = 		inla(formula, family="gaussian", data = yX)
summary(mod)

the extraconstr will ensure that t[1] = 0, but it will introduce a
singularlity in the model, but it should go through.

Another way, is to introduce a very presice observation, that t[1] is
'observed' to be zero. this can be a second likelihood. this is better,
as it does not correspond to a singularily.

I know, 'common in time series litterature', there is so much 'strange'
there... the correct way, is to start from the marginal distribution
for t[1], and then conditional from that point. this is the exact way.
both AR1 and AR(p) is implemented like that.

H

messages.body_plain:
Hi Finn,

Thanks so much for your detailed response. That's really helpful.

I had been playing with the `inla.mesh.assessment` tool, but I wasn't exactly sure whether I should  be monitoring at `sd` or `sd.dev <http://sd.dev>`. It's much clearer now, especially with the `inlabru` ggplot tools. Really nice, thanks!

My reasoning was that I was worried that my boundary was too wiggly and this may have been causing numerical issues related to the triangles shape and size in difficult areas. I thought a more simplified non-convex hull could fix this, but I was concerned that over simplification would modify the geographic boundaries and negate the benefits of the barrier model by allowing smoothing and borrowing of strength from areas that are actually ocean, or discontiguous land areas. But like you say, as long as the geometry of the hull is close enough to the actual geometry it should hopefully be ok.

Using the `inla.mesh.assessment` tool both meshes (using either the shapefile as a boundary or the hull) look to be OK, they both exhibit constant variance throughout
the domain of interest. I think I will go ahead with the hull mesh, because it is a bit less complex and has more uniform triangles, so will hopefully be more numerically stable/accurate.

Thanks again for your help. I'll be back with more questions!

Cheers,

Mike

On Tuesday, June 5, 2018 at 6:57:21 PM UTC+1, Finn Lindgren wrote:

> Hi,
>
> the main effect of the barrier model is to eliminate the Neumann
> boundary effects at the edge of a mesh by allowing the parameters to
> change outside a domain of interest instead of just extending the mesh
> beyond the domain of interest (which can't be done when the domain
> extension would intrude on the domain of interest, such as for
> islands, peninsulas, etc).  The number, sizes, and shapes of triangles
> instead controls the numerical approximation properties of the
> resulting discretised model, in much the same way for both
> alternatives for handling the boundary, so they can largely be treated
> as unrelated issues.
>
> As long as the geometry used to define the barrier in the barrier
> model is close enough to your real geometry you should be fine.  It is
> relatively safe to move a _convex_ boundary outwards for the barrier
> model, but it's
> concave parts (like islands) where you would get noticeable
> differences when over-simplifying the boundary/barrier.
>
> I'd recommend taking a look at the meshbuilder() tool for
> interactively exploring mesh quality in relation to computational
> approximation properties.
> The important parts can also be accessed directly for any mesh,
> through the inla.mesh.assessment() function, that evaluates the
> pointwise standard deviations
> for a specified correlation range in a basic SPDE/GMRF/Matern model.
> A numerically accurate model would have a constant variance throughout
> the domain of interest.
> The barrier models are a bit more forgiving at the barriers, but the
> tool should still give a good idea of the required triangle sizes.
> The usually appropriate quantity to plot is "sd.dev <http://sd.dev>", which is an
> estimate of the ratio between the pointwise variances of the discrete
> model and the desired continuous domain model.
> Currently, the function returns "sd", "sd.dev <http://sd.dev>", and "edge.len", which
> is the average triangle edge length near each location (mostly just
> informational).
>
> The example below uses the ggplot2 features from inlabru (see
> http://github.com/fbachl/inlabru for installation instructions; either
> CRAN or the more bug-fixed development version) to illustrate this.
> (The interactive meshbuilder tool has more options, but doesn't handle
> spherical meshes; inla.mesh.assessment also doesn't fully handle that
> case, but will currently just show you one side of the sphere...)
>
> bnd <- inla.mesh.segment(cbind(c(0, 10, 10, 0, 0),
>                                c(0, 0, 10, 10, 0)), bnd = TRUE)
> mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary = bnd, max.edge = 1)
> out <- inla.mesh.assessment(mesh, spatial.range = 3, alpha = 2)
>
> ggplot2::ggplot() + inlabru::gg(out, mapping=aes_(col=~sd.dev <http://sd.dev>))
>
> To build a spherical mesh, you just need to convert the
> longitude-latitude cutoff&max.edge parameters to radians (multiply by
> pi/180), and supply
>   crs = inla.CRS("sphere")
> to inla.mesh.2d(), which will automatically transform inputs with
> proper crs info (so you'll need to specify a crs=inla.CRS("longlat")
> when you construct the nonconvex hull).
>
> One can in principle compute the same assessment directly for the
> chosen barrier model, but the barrier models weren't around when the
> meshbuilder assessment code was written, so it needs to go on the TODO
> list.
>
> Finn
>
>
>
> On 5 June 2018 at 18:11,  <mike.bl...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi all,
> >
> >
> >
> > I am new to INLA, but I have spent the last couple of weeks reading and
> > playing with the various tutorials and the documentation. I feel that I have
> > got to grips with the basics of the software. Thanks to you all for
> > producing so much awesome documentation for this amazing package!
> >
> >
> >
> > I would like to ask you experts and other users for some guidance and advice
> > on my model. I apologise that this is such a long post! Please just respond
> > to whatever you can/have time to.
> >
> >
> >
> > My model is a species distribution model predicting the probability of
> > occurrence of a species of insect as a function of various bioclimatic and
> > demographic variables at a global scale. The data are presence/absence
> > (~15,000 observations). The covariates are mostly raster data with a 5km*5km
> > global resolution (WorldClim). The model has a binomial likelihood, some
> > fixed effects covariates and a barrier.model spde spatial random effect:
> >
> >
> >
> > y ~ b0 + BIOC_1 + BIOC_2 + ... + BIOC_p + f(s, model = barrier.spde) - 1
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > I have quite a few questions(!), but first I would like to ask for some
> > advice on mesh building at a global scale.
> >
> >
> >
> > To start with I took a shapefile of global coastlines. I simplified the
> > polygons (using gSimplify from rgeos) and removed all the small islands
> > below a specific area size. The aim of this was to try to avoid too complex
> > a shape, so I can achieve nice uniform triangulation in my sampling domain.
> > I then used these spatial polygons to define the inner boundary of the mesh,
> > and used the observation points as initial vertices for the triangles.
> > (Currently I am using decimal degrees, which I appreciate is inappropriate
> > at a global scale, but I just wanted to get my head around the mesh building
> > before implementing the spherical mesh).
> >
> >
> >
> > ## Domain boundary
> >
> >   bndry <- inla.sp2segment(
> >
> >   shape,
> >
> >   crs = crs(shape)
> >
> > )
> >
> > ## Mesh
> >
> > mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(
> >
> >   loc = coords.est,
> >
> >   boundary = bndry,
> >
> >   cutoff = max.edge.length/5,
> >
> >   max.edge = c(1, 5) * max.edge.length,
> >
> >   min.angle = 21
> >
> > )
> >
> >
> >
> > However, the observations have a pretty extreme non-random distribution.
> > They are very clumped in certain areas. Using these locations as initial
> > vertices seemed to be problematic, resulting in very high number of
> > triangles and general bad mesh patterns (even when using a relatively high
> > cutoff).
> >
> >
> >
> > Next, after reading Finn's recommendation in this post, I decided to try a
> > uniform inner triangulation (not using the observation points). This reduced
> > the number of triangles and I can produce what I think seems like an OK
> > mesh. After first running the model with a relatively coarse mesh to get an
> > idea of the spatial range, the final mesh$n is ~10,000. (with an estimated
> > spatial range of 10 degrees and max.edge = ~2 degrees).
> >
> > Then I ran my model using int.strategy = "eb", strategy = "gaussian"  and
> > diagonal = 1000 to get some computationally cheap initial values to feed the
> > proper model (using auto and simplified lapace) and every seems good, but
> > then when I run the proper model, it seems to struggle. I get the 'stupid
> > search' and my DIC is inf. This made me wonder that my mesh is too poor and
> > it is causing numerical issues?
> >
> >
> >
> > So, worried that my mesh is too complex. I read this post, and tried
> > defining an arbitrary nonconvex hull as my boundary, rather than the
> > shapefile itself.
> >
> >
> >
> > ## Non-convex hull domain boundary
> >
> > nc.hull <- inla.nonconvex.hull(
> >
> >             coords.est,
> >
> >             convex = 3,
> >
> >             concave = 3,
> >
> >             resolution = 150)
> >
> > ## Mesh.nc
> >
> > mesh.nc <http://mesh.nc> <- inla.mesh.2d(
> >
> >   boundary = nc.hull,
> >
> >   cutoff = max.edge.length/5,  # make max.edge/5 for full resolution
> >
> >   max.edge = c(1, 3) * max.edge.length,
> >
> >   # offset = 1, #c(max.edge.length, outer.boundary),
> >
> >   min.angle = 20
> >
> > )
> >
> >
> >
> > This results in a mesh$n of ~5000 and a much more uniform 'good' look. But I
> > am worried that altering the geographic structure makes the barrier method
> > somewhat pointless?
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > I would really appreciate some guidance or insight on the best way to
> > approach this mesh building. I would like to be able to find the good
> > trade-off between mesh complexity and computational expense! Apologies if I
> > have made any glaring errors or oversights...
> >
> > and apologies for rambling...
> >
> >
> >
> > Thanks for taking the time to read this far :)
> >
> >
> >
> > Cheers,
> >
> >
> >
> > Mike

  Days_spent_making_campign  + Categories + County +
  f(state_codes, model = "bym", graph = USA.adj, diagonal = 1e-4) +

  f(year1, model = "iid") +

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am sorry, I have replied only to you. I am including it in the list again because I am not able to answer you properly.

So, you are probably right, the advanced example in page 9 is a mixture of a degenerate distribution {P(Y=0)=1} with a truncated Poisson {P(Y=y | Y > 0)}, (type 0 model) and you are able to add a linear term to the zero-inflated probability using the clever trick of two likelihoods described in the example.

The type 2 (page 10) seems to be another thing, where instead of having the zero-inflated probability directly as type 1 model, you have the alpha parameter, you also have x which I am not sure exactly how you can add the linear term.

Cheers,
Leo

messages.subject: inla.fmesher.write.file() error on cluster
messages.subject_clean: inla.fmesher.write.file() error on cluster
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm trying to fit a basic logistic regression model with one random effect, but the number of rows in my data frame is about 9 million. I'm running this on a cluster and keep getting the following error:

Error in file(filename, "wb") : cannot open the connection
Calls: inla -> inla.write.fmesher.file -> file
In addition: There were 50 or more warnings (use warnings() to see the first 50)

The IT person in my department and I think this is likely related to INLA writing temporary files that are too large for the /tmp directory on the cluster (which has much smaller memory than the node itself).

Is there a way to change the directory to which INLA writes tmp files? Or perhaps a way to control how much memory these files take up.

Thanks,

Jessica Godwin

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have the following log-log model:

reports = Intercept + beta* logpop + f(year, model = "rw1")

reports refer to the number of damages caused by the species A

logpop refers to the population size (log transformation) of the species A

I have 16 years of data and one data point for each year. I have used PC prior (1, 0.05)

I am studying how population size of species A affects the number of damages in agricultural crops, and I want to investigate the possible outcomes and probabilities of success of different interventions of population control.

I have the following model:

M <- reports ~  logpop + f(year,

                            model = "rw1" ,

                            scale.model = TRUE,

                            hyper = list(

                              theta = list (

                                prior = "pc.prec",

                                param = c(1,0.05))))

I2 <- inla(M,

           lincomb = lcb,

           control.inla=list(lincomb.derived.only=FALSE),

           control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE),

           family = "nbinomial",

           data = MyDataset,control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, link = 1))

The lincomb object is set to get the effect of population size over the number of damages

MyData <- data.frame(logpop = seq(min(MyDataset $logpop),max(MyDataset $logpop),length=16))

Xmat <- model.matrix(~ logpop,data=MyData)

Xmat <- as.data.frame(Xmat)

lcb <- inla.make.lincombs(Xmat)

To get the expected values,

MyData <- cbind (GridCovariates,I2$summary.lincomb[,c("mean","0.025quant","0.975quant")])

Pred.marg <- I2$marginals.lincomb.derived

MyData$mu <- unlist(lapply(Pred.marg,function(x) inla.emarginal(exp,x)))

MyData$selo <- unlist( lapply( Pred.marg, function(x) inla.qmarginal(c(0.025), inla.tmarginal(exp, x))))

MyData$seup <- unlist( lapply(Pred.marg,function(x) inla.qmarginal(c(0.975), inla.tmarginal(exp, x))))

Now, I want to know 1) how different interventions of population control would affect the reduction of damage; and 2) which is the probability of success for a certain intervention.

In JAGGS, I would compute the prediction of number of damages for an initial population size a, and the prediction of number of damages for a population size b (after being reduced, let’s say 10%). Then, I would compute the difference between the predictions and calculate ecdf (empirical cumulative distribution function) to investigate the probability for the intervention to succeed.

But in R-INLA I am having some troubles.

1)      With question 1, how do I get the expected outcomes of number of damages for a given population size? It should be an easy one, but it’s driving me crazy.

2)      With question 2, how do I compute the difference between the predictions in R-INLA to get the final ecdf for the difference?

Thanks,

/ Teresa

messages.body_plain:
Hi there ,

I am trying to fit a model with a space time applications . My dataset consists of more than 9'000 data points collected at 9'000 different geolocation (longitude, latitude). For each data point I have two covariates : week of the Year (woy) and Year and a binary response variable .
I have tried a joint space-time model : SPDE for space , ar1 model for the group woy and replicated in Year (independent in year ) . However, it required way too much memory !

So now, I would like to model the space and the time separately.

Consider the following model :

form2 <-  Presence ~ -1 + b0 + f(s, model=spde.a)+f(Week, model ='ar1')+f(Year, model ='ar1')

Pm <- inla(form2, family='binomial', data=inla.stack.data(stk.2),
           control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk.2), compute=TRUE),
           control.inla=list(strategy='laplace'),
           control.compute=list(dic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE,waic=TRUE))

To simplify let's have the simplified dataset  :

Location Year Week
s1 2006 26
s2 2006 26
s3 2006 27
s4 2006 28
s5 2006 28
s6 2006 29
s7 2006 29
s8 2006 30
s9 2007 26
s10 2007 27
s11 2007 27
s12 2007 28
s13 2007 29
s14 2007 29

The AR1 process is of the form : x_i,t = p_i x_i(t-1) + Eit         Eit ~iidN(0,alpha)

What I don't understand is the computation behind the AR1 (and similarly for RW1,RW2)  as I have multiple non unique Time points that are non nested in Year(I have multiple observations by week for each year)   but rather in space ( which I can't model here ) . How can local OLS works in that case ?

Thank you in advance :)

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I was drawn to check out "inlabru" because it seems like it would be of use for the bird count data I work with. I have previously published a chapter of my dissertation which used R-INLA for the North American Breeding Bird Survey data set: https://pubs.er.usgs.gov/publication/70179080

For my current analysis, I am hoping to assess guild-level response but allowing slope to vary by species, to see the nuance in species' response while still assessing the response of the guild. So for example, my data frame looks like...

Survey_Route Year    Species                        Guild                            Count CovariateX
001                   1986  Rusty blackbird            short-distance migrant  5        0.9
001                   1987  Rusty blackbird            short-distance migrant  7        0.5
001                   1987  Blackburnian warbler   long-distance migrant   2        0.5
002                   1986  Blackburnian warbler   long-distance migrant   8        0.2

So for this hypothetical, I want to estimate the coefficient of Co-variate X for each guild, but within the model, I also want to assess how each species' response deviates from the guild response.

I had an R-INLA formulation to do this like...
f(species, CovariateX, model = 'iid')

I'm not sure how to translate this for inlabru, though.

I found an example with spatial modeling...

cmp = lethal ~ Intercept+
   myspde(map = coordinates,
   group = Year,
   ngroup = nyear,
   model = inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh, alpha=1.5, prior.range=c(0.1,0.01), prior.sigma=c(1,0.01)),
   mesh = mesh,
   control.group=list(model="ar1"))

I'm wondering if that's how the formulation would change, but also with the note that as far as I can understand how to apply this (which might be wrong) I have several other "grouping factors," such as year. Also, my previous models weren't spatially explicit but I'm thinking about moving to that framework to deal with auto-correlation. So, any advice on formulation of multilevel models in inlabru is much appreciated!

Thanks,
Jess

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

just to check, if you use group=g, then 'g' needs to be integers 1,2,3,
 in case you set group=Year directly, it needs to be group=Year-
min(Year)+1

the model 'ar1' is a little tricky, as it assumes the locations (or
values) to be unit spaced, like

f(Week, model="ar1")

and passing in Week=c(1,11,12,33)

it simply assume that these are at time points 1,2,3,4. in such cases
you can force that the time points are weeks, by adding

	values=1:52

for which the model is an ar1 on 1, 2, ..., 52, where the value at time
point 1, 11, 12 and 33 are used in the models.

if you do not want to agument the AR1 model with many un-used points,
there is an alternative continous time version, model='ou', which do
the same. in this case, f(Week, model='ou') would behave as one would
expect

H

Hi,
we haven't set up a separate mailing list for inlabru yet, but I try
to respond to inlabru specific questions that appear here.

Factors still have shaky support, but if you first convert them to
indices (from 1 to #levels) the inla() and bru() models below are
equivalent:

data <- data.frame(mycov = rnorm(20), myfactor=c(1:10, 1:10))
data$y <- data$mycov * rnorm(10)[data$myfactor] + rnorm(20, sd = 0.01)

res <- inla(formula = y ~ -1 + f(myfactor, mycov, model="iid"), data=data)

res2 <- bru(~ -1 + eff(map=myfactor, model="iid", n=10), data=data,
     like("gaussian", formula = y ~ mycov * eff))

summary(res)
INLA:::summary.inla(res2)

Finn

On Thu, 2018-06-14 at 04:56 -0700, endale alemayehu wrote:
> Dear all INLA Group Members,
>
> This is kindly to ask you the following questions.
> Please, kindly give your comment to all questions you are familiar to
> discuss.
>
> 1. In my study, I have the objective to compare the results of INLA
> and MCMC; thus, what technique will I use for comparison (DIC, error
> term) or other techniques of comparison?

the common approach is to compare the marginal distributions, ie the
ones computed/approximated with INLA and the one that is estimated from
the MCMC output. You have to be very careful to ensure that the two
models are *the same*... if you run with a simulated example with high
counts, then the poisson = normal and both INLA and mcmc should be the
same.

> 2. Since, my data is expected to follow Poisson distribution, can I
> compare with negative binomial (provided that to check if there
> is over-dispersion of the data across region)

you can. the neg.binom is an extention of the poisson to allow for
overdispersion. you need a prior for the overdispersion that contract
the neg.binom to the poission (see the paper by Simpson et al 2017, in
Statistical Science and penalized complexity priors)

> 3. Is it possible to compare model with different prior (may be
> default with PC prior).

you can do that to check for prior robustness.

>
> 4. To check the effect of explanatory variables I need to fit models
> as  intercept only model then including all the fixed variables and
> finally including both the fixed effect and random effect; so can I
> compare the results of those model by using DIC?

you can. also the WAIC criterion is there and its better theoretically
motivated.

Best
H

messages.body_plain:
That would be equivalent to
(CovA + CovB) * eff
which is probably not what you want?
There are two possible situation, depending on if you want the same variance for the effects or not. If you want one precision parameter for each of them, then just define two effects, effA and effB, and use them as
CovA*effA + CovB*effB

For a common precision, I’m not actually sure how to do it in a simple way in inlabru; in raw INLA one can use the “copy” feature with fixed scaling, or construct a model with inla.stack(), but I’d need to see a concrete use case to figure it out for inlabru (I suspect it would require a new feature in the interface, or a more complex construction in the formula).

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] GAMMA REGRESSION
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] GAMMA REGRESSION
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

the "gamma" likelihood is parameterised in a way that appears to not
match either the general or specific beta=1 case.

Further, the general case uses two predictors in one likelihood, so
isn't possible in the current implementation.

The special parameterisation of the precision (see the pdf on
r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org>, http://www.math.ntnu.no/inla/r-inla.org/doc/likelihood/gamma.pdf)
leads to (for a user-specified "scale" vector):
  b[i] = scale[i] * phi / mu[i]^2
so that doesn't allow fixing beta.
However, since scale can be different for each observation, an
iterated approximation may be possible, similar to the inlabru
approach.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA users,

After correcting the error noticed by Elias, I thought the code would be ok, but I recently noticed that I was doing something else wrong. I attach an updated simulation based on the latest spde tutorial to reproduce my problem. I pressume the problem is on the observation matrix (inla.spde.make.A()) that I pass to the the inla.stack(). I also add a possible solution to the problem, but I am not very convinced.

I noticed this when changing the side of the scaling parameter in the PS model. So, with my previous code this one runs:
form_covar2 <- y ~ 0 + b0.pp + b0.y +  f(covariate.pp, model="rw1") + f(covariate.y, copy='covariate.pp', fixed=FALSE)
But this one doesn't:
form_covar1 <- y ~ 0 + b0.pp + b0.y +  f(covariate.y, model="rw2") + f(covariate.pp, copy='covariate.y', fixed=FALSE)
"Error in inla(form_covar1, family = c("gaussian", "poisson"), data = inla.stack.data(j.stk), :
  f(covariate.pp). Covariate does not match 'values' 9 times. Indexes for mismatch:139 141 146 149 150 152 157 158 162. This is not what you want. Use NA values in the covariate!"

As I mentioned, I do also add a possible solution at the very end of the code but I pressume there is still something wrong since fitted effects do differ significantly when I "copy" the pp effect on the marks and viceversa.

I hope this is useful to other people too. Thanks very much,
Iosu

On Monday, March 14, 2016 at 10:52:31 AM UTC+1, Elias T. Krainski wrote:

>
> On 13/03/16 12:38, Iosu Paradinas wrote:
> > "Covariate does not match 'values' X times. Indexes for mismatch..."
>
> The problem is not related to the stack functionality instead due to the fact that you did use inla.group() twice and tried to copy one from the other. In order to have it working you do need to do the same discretization/grouping for the covariate. You may do something like:
>   covariate.ppy.g <- inla.group(c(covariate.pp, covariate.y))
> and them use the first nv + n.c values for the 'pp' stack:
>                                         covariate.pp=covariate.ppy.g[1:(nv+n.c)])))
> and the last n.v values for the 'y' stack
>                                        covariate.y=covariate.ppy.g[nv+1:n.c])))
>
>
> Elias

messages.subject: SPDE overfitting?
messages.subject_clean: SPDE overfitting?
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I have developed a binomial GLM (log link) with a PC matern spatial random effect to predict the distribution of a species of insect at a global scale.

At the moment my model seems to be over-fitting rather drastically. I think this is due to the spatial random effect taking over; the scale
of the random effect (posterior sigma u) is high compared to the environmental covariates, the number of number of effective parameters
is high and the number of equivalent replicates is low. The map of the fitted values (probability of presence) shows quite drastic over-fitting.

I have been trying to address this by reducing the scale of the spatial effect with better prior choices on the spde, but I have so far been unable to alter its behaviour.
I have found this other thread <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/r-inla-discussion-group/cPU0iJA2UqY/z774i9H2AwAJ> helpful as we appear to have experienced a similar scenario, but I appear to be a bit stuck with this. I would like to ask for some advice.

I have taken the approach described in Illian et al (2012) to choose a prior range that offers a similar level of smoothing to that of the environmental covariates. This
was to try to make sure that the spatial effect would operate at a longer range and not explain variation that could be explained by the covariates. From comparing
plots of the spatial field computed using a range of priors, a prior range of 10 degrees appears to be reasonable. Considering this I set the mesh max edge length
to ~1 degree, following the advice that estimation should be unbiased if the mesh resolution is ~1/10 of the spatial range. (The values are all converted from degrees to
radians for the spherical mesh).
Regarding the prior on the standard deviation, because in the binomial (logit) model the spatial effect is multiplicative with the mean, I set the prior sigma to log(1.1),
assuming an average of 10% +/- effect on the predicted mean spatial effect.
I have applied the default N(0, 1e4) to the priors on the regression coefficients.

These hyperpriors result in posterior estimates for the range of ~13 degrees, which I think makes sense, but posterior sigma u of ~2.5, despite a prior of log(1.1) ~= 0.04. This is even
after heavily constraining the spatial effect with the tail probability on the prior sigma [i.e. prior.sigma = c(log(1.1), 0.01)].

Altering these priors (much larger/smaller range etc) seems to have little effect on the results, the posterior fitted estimates follow almost exactly the data.

Below I copy some of the code I have used to create the estimation model and I have attached the verbose output. I use a prediction stack for the predictions, but I didn't include that yet to
avoid too long a post, I can provide the full code and the data if that would help.

Any help or insight as to where I am going wrong is greatly appreciated!

Thanks for all the invaluable help available through this forum!

Mike

#----------------------------------------------------------------------Data ####
world_map <- _a simplified SpatialPolygonsDataframe_
data <- _a SpatialPointsDataframe of presence points and corresponding covariates values, nrow ~20,000_
cov_rst <- _a raster stack of covariates_
## Format for model
cov_names <-  c("tsi", "BIO16", "BIO17", "ghf")  # covariates of interest (continuous variables)
data <- data[c("presence", cov_names)]
cov_rst <- raster::subset(cov_rst, cov_names, drop = T)
cov_est <- data@data[cov_names]
loc_est <- inla.mesh.map(data@coords, projection = "longlat")  # convert lat/lon to 3D xyz
y <- data$presence

#----------------------------------------------------------------------Mesh ####
## Domain boundary
boundary <- inla.sp2segment(world_map,
                            crs = inla.CRS("longlat"))
## Mesh parameters
range <- 10
max_edge <- range/10 * pi/180
kCut_off <- 0.5
min_angle <- 26
## Build mesh
(mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(
  boundary = boundary,
  cutoff = max_edge * kCut_off,
  max.edge = c(1, 5) * max_edge,  # (inner, outer)
  min.angle = min_angle,
  crs = inla.CRS("sphere")))$n
[1] 32795
## Plot mesh
plot(mesh$mesh, rgl = T)

#----------------------------------------------------------Projector matrix ####
A_est <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc = as.matrix(loc_est))

#----------------------------------------------------------------SPDE model ####
## Hyperparameter priors
prior_range0 <- 10
prior_sigmau0 <- log(1.1)
alpha <- 2
## SPDE model
spde = inla.spde2.pcmatern(
  mesh = mesh,
  alpha = alpha,
  prior.range = c(prior_range0 * (pi/180), 0.1),  # p(spatial range < prior.range0)
  prior.sigma = c(prior_sigmau0, 0.01),  # p(sigma > prior.sigma.u0)
  )

#----------------------------------------------------------Estimation stack ####
stack_est <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = y),
  effects = list(s = 1:spde$n.spde,  # spatial random effect index
                 list(b0 = 1,  # intercept
                      cov_est)),  # covariates
  A = list(A_est, 1),
  tag = 'est')

#------------------------------------------------------------------Formulae ####
coef_names <- stack_est$effects$names[2:length(stack_est$effects$names)]
## Fixed effects only
form_fx <- formula(paste("y ~ -1 +", paste(coef_names, collapse = "+")))
## Fixed effects and spatial random effect
form_full <- update.formula(
  form_fx, ~. +
  f(s, model = spde))
> form_full
y ~ b0 + tsi + BIO16 + BIO17 + ghf + f(s, model = spde) - 1

#----------------------------------------------------------Estimation model ####
mdl_est = inla(
  formula = form_full,
  family = "binomial",
  data = inla.stack.data(stack_est),
  control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack_est),
                           compute = F),
  control.family = list(control.link = list(model = "logit")),
  control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb",  # empirical bayes (cheap computation for testing)
                      strategy = "gaussian",   # (cheap computation for testing)
                      correct = F,  # correction to improve laplace approximations for binary data
                      correct.factor = 1),  # default = 1, report uses 10

messages.subject: GroupRho interpretation
messages.subject_clean: GroupRho interpretation
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I’ve constructed a series of different space-time models using matern spde for the spatial components and AR1 processes for the time-steps.  Each of the models is fit with a joint binomial-gamma likelihood.  In a few instances (3 of 44 different models), I note that the GroupRho returned for the gamma level is greater than 1 (i.e., 1.020715647, 1.354702025, 1.115073724).  The GroupRho for the other models, which are similarly constructed with comparable data, range from 0.97-0.99.  All other outputs/results are as expected/anticipated.

Is it typical for the GroupRho correlation estimate to exceed 1 or is this indicative of an error somewhere?

Thanks,
John

messages.body_plain:
On Wed, 2018-06-27 at 08:00 -0700, Ecographica wrote:
> Hello,
>
> I’ve constructed a series of different space-time models using matern
> spde for the spatial components and AR1 processes for the time-

> steps.  Each of the models is fit with a joint binomial-gamma

> likelihood.  In a few instances (3 of 44 different models), I note
> that the GroupRho returned for the gamma level is greater than 1
> (i.e., 1.020715647, 1.354702025, 1.115073724).  The GroupRho for the
> other models, which are similarly constructed with comparable data,
> range from 0.97-0.99.  All other outputs/results are as
> expected/anticipated.
>
> Is it typical for the GroupRho correlation estimate to exceed 1 or is
> this indicative of an error somewhere?
>

this is a bit weird, but how the densities are represeted internally,
this *could* happen if the density does not goes to zero at one end.
the internal representation does not know any hard limits, so this has
to come in automatically (by the zero density at the limit)

the failsafe option, is to look at the marginals for GroupRho in the
internal scale, meaning

rho = 2*exp(theta)/(1+exp(theta)) -1

and then the density is wrt theta. its here

> r=inla(y~1,data=data.frame(y=1:10))
> str(r$internal.marginals.hyperpar)
List of 1
 $ Log precision for the Gaussian observations: num [1:75, 1:2] -6.28
-5.42 -4.57 -4.15 -3.93 ...
  ..- attr(*, "hyperid")= chr "65001|INLA.Data1"
  ..- attr(*, "dimnames")=List of 2
  .. ..$ : NULL
  .. ..$ : chr [1:2] "x" "y"

in a simple example, this is the density writ theta = log(precision)

let me know, if this does not solve your issue

H

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
It sounds like your model needs a lot of memory (common for space-time models...).
If you see how much memory it uses for num.threads=1, a very rough estimate of the required multithreaded memory is to multiply that with your desired num.threads value.

(It’s a bit more complicated than that due to nested multithreading in some cases, but I think the current version doesn’t do that for large models.)

Finn

messages.subject: fish distribution based on a stream network
messages.subject_clean: fish distribution based on a stream network
messages.body_plain:
All,
I was hoping to get some advice on how to proceed with developing a fish distribution model based on presence/absence data with the GIS attributes as covariates. I was able to develop this model using SPDE in INLA with a 2d mesh by using the geo-referenced fish presence/absence data and covariates using logistic regression.  However, when using the 2d mesh, I had a lot of vertices that were not informative since they were not on the stream network, which was not supplied since I only used the points. Also, without the stream network, INLA calculated the Euclidean distances between points.

I would like to use stream distance as measured between the points and not use Euclidean distance. My questions are:
1) Is there a way to import a large stream network more than 10,000km of stream with 3,000 sampling points in INLA?
2) If so can I use a 1d mesh based on the stream network to calculated the stream distance in INLA? If this is possible does anyone have an example of creating 1d mesh using a dendritic network (e.g. stream or roads).
3) I am most interested in inference for the data supplied not using INLA to predict to unsampled locations (I can predict outside of INLA), if this is a simpler solution.
4) If the approach I am proposing is problematic, I can calculate stream distance outside INLA and if so is there way to utilize the SPDE approach?

Thanks in advance for your consideration.

Dan

messages.subject_clean: Predictions INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

thanks for your email. There isn't anything strange going on: If x[i]
is not observed, it is simply integrated out conditioned on the data
that is observed. The values of NA is interpreted different if an
observation is NA or a component is NA,

y ~ 1 + x + f(idx)

if y[1] = NA, then its not observed so there is no likelihood
contribtion related to y[1]

if x[1] = NA, then there is no effect of x for linear.predictor[1], so
this is eqv to x[1] = 0

if idx[1] = NA, then there is no effect of 'f' for linear.preditor[1]

H
